title: A Cut Is Not a Knockout

scenes.tts: You cut both copies of a gene in every cell of a dish. Why is half the dish still making the protein? Look at one cell. It comes from a diploid line, so it carries two copies of the gene. We aim Cas nine at both copies. The cut is the easy part. What the cell does next is the real question.

scenes.visual: A dish of 100 cells is cut, a question appears, one cell zooms in showing two gene copies; Cas9 cuts both.

scenes.tts: Cas nine is aimed by a guide. The target-binding part of the guide is twenty nucleotides long. It must sit right next to a short motif called the P A M. The P A M reads N G G. Cas nine ignored DNA that matched the guide but had no nearby P A M. In the original test, the cut fell three base pairs upstream of the P A M.
scenes.caption: Cas9 is aimed by a guide. The target-binding part of the guide is 20 nucleotides long. It must sit right next to a short motif called the PAM. The PAM reads NGG. scenes.visual: A DNA letter strand: 20 letters under a blue guide, three orange PAM letters beside them; PAM letters swapped for a non-PAM and crossed out, then restored; a cut line lands three letters from the PAM.

scenes.tts: The cut is where your control ends. The cell repairs the break on its own. One route is end joining. It needs no template. It can leave insertions and deletions. Another route is homology directed repair. It copies a template that you supply. So sequencing the pool shows a spread of different alleles.

scenes.visual: A broken strand rejoins with an inserted letter, then with a deleted letter; a template route is named; the scene ends on six rows of alleles.

scenes.tts: Now count the alleles in the pool. Ten percent are unedited. Thirty-five percent lose one base pair. Twenty-five percent gain one. Fifteen percent lose three, five percent lose six, and ten percent lose seven. A length that is not a multiple of three shifts the frame. Lose one, gain one and lose seven all shift it. Add them up. Seventy percent are frameshifted.

scenes.tts: Each cell has two alleles. Assume they are edited independently. The chance that one allele is frameshifted is zero point seven. For both, multiply. Zero point seven times zero point seven is zero point four nine. So forty-nine percent of cells have both alleles frameshifted. About half the cells still carry at least one in-frame or unedited allele.
scenes.caption: Each cell has two alleles. Assume they are edited independently. The chance that one allele is frameshifted is 0.7. For both, multiply. 0.7 times 0.7 is 0.49. So 49 percent of cells have both alleles frameshifted. About half the cells still carry at least one in-frame or unedited allele.
scenes.visual: A 10 by 10 square of cells; a red band of 70 percent for allele one and another for allele two; their overlap, 0.49, is the cells with both alleles frameshifted.

scenes.tts: So a cut, a mutated allele, and a knockout are three different states. Only the third is a genetic result. A pool like this is a mosaic, not a null. Derive clones and genotype them, or use more than one guide, before you call the phenotype a knockout.
